title: Friction, Drag and Elasticity
learning_objectives: Compute the kinetic and static friction forces and know which one applies.
Explain what drag is and how it depends on speed.
Relate stress and strain in a material, and use Hooke's law.

sections.title: Introduction: Further Applications of Newton's Laws
objectives: Describe how friction, drag and elasticity each enter Newton's laws.

misconceptions.claim: Newton's second law is the last word on any force.
misconceptions.correction: It is the rule that connects the forces to the motion. Friction, drag and elasticity are three of the forces it is applied to.

summary: Newton's second law applies to any force, once the force is known.
This chapter takes three of them: friction, drag and the force in a spring.
Each one resists motion, and each one has its own rule.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Friction
objectives: Tell static friction from kinetic friction and compute the friction force.
Use the coefficient of friction with the normal force.

misconceptions.claim: Friction is always the same force, whatever the weight on the surface.
misconceptions.correction: The maximum static friction is proportional to the normal force, so a heavier object presses harder and the friction limit rises with it.

summary: Static friction adjusts itself up to a limit, then the object slides.
Kinetic friction has a steady value once the object is sliding.
Both are set by the normal force and the coefficient of friction.

sections.title: Drag Forces
objectives: Explain what drag is and how it grows with speed.
Sketch the drag force against speed for low and for high speed.

misconceptions.claim: Drag is a small force that only matters for very fast objects.
misconceptions.correction: At low speeds the drag grows with the square of the speed, so doubling the speed quadruples it. It matters for anything that moves through air at speed.

summary: Drag opposes the motion and always points against the velocity.
At low speeds the drag is small and grows with the square of the speed.
At high speeds the drag grows faster still.

sections.title: Elasticity: Stress and Strain
objectives: Define stress and strain, and use Hooke's law for a spring.
Tell the elastic limit, the yield point and the breaking point apart.

misconceptions.claim: A spring stretches a little and then springs back, no matter how hard you pull.
misconceptions.correction: Not past the elastic limit. Beyond it the material does not return to its original shape, and beyond the breaking point it fails altogether.

summary: Stress is force over area. Strain is the change in length over the original length.
Hooke's law holds while the material stays in the elastic region.
The elastic limit, the yield point and the breaking point mark three different failures.

definition.text: The friction force that acts on a body at rest, between zero and the maximum the surface allows.
The friction force on a body that is sliding, proportional to the normal force.
The contact force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself, which sets the size of the friction force.
The resistive force a fluid exerts on a body moving through it, always opposite to the motion.
The force per unit area applied to a material.
The fractional change in length of a material under stress.
